title: Price analysis: is the price fair and reasonable?
summary: Before you award, the contracting officer must decide the price is fair and reasonable. Price analysis checks the total price without looking at the contractor's costs, mainly by comparing it with other prices. It is the most common pricing tool you will use.
why: Price or Cost Analysis is 10 exam questions, pricing is the weakest area on past exams (which is why CON 7300V was added), and you will do price analysis on almost every buy.

sections.body:
- **Price analysis:** examines and evaluates a proposed price **without** evaluating its separate cost elements and profit (FAR 15.404-1). Used whenever certified cost or pricing data are not required.
- **Cost analysis:** looks at each cost element and the profit (15.404-2). Required when certified cost or pricing data are required, and useful in other cases.

Fair and reasonable means fair to both sides: not too high for the Government and not unreasonably low for the contractor to perform.

FAR 15.404-1 lists techniques; the first two are preferred:
1. Comparison of proposed prices received in response to the solicitation (adequate price competition is usually enough on its own).
2. Comparison with prior prices paid for the same or similar items, adjusted for time (inflation), quantity and terms.
3. Parametric estimates and rough yardsticks, such as dollars per pound or per square foot.
4. Comparison with competitive published price lists, catalogs and market prices.
5. Comparison with the independent Government cost estimate (IGCE).
6. Comparison with prices found through market research.
7. Analysis of data other than certified cost or pricing data provided by the offeror.

Price competition exists when two or more responsible offerors, competing independently, submit priced offers that meet the requirement, award goes to the best value with price a substantial factor, and there is no finding that the price of the otherwise successful offer is unreasonable (15.403-2(c)(1)). When that is true, the competition itself is strong evidence the price is reasonable.

On simplified buys the contracting officer still determines the price is fair and reasonable, based on competitive quotes where possible (FAR 12.204, 13.203). With only one quote, use other evidence: catalog prices, prior purchases, market research or an IGCE, and write down what you used. Micro-purchases need no competitive quotes if the price is reasonable.

Unbalanced pricing means one or more line items are significantly overstated or understated, even though the total looks fine. It is risky when, for example, early items are overpriced (front-loading) or quantity estimates are wrong. Analyze it, and reject an offer when the lack of balance poses an unacceptable risk (15.404-6).
Write a short price reasonableness determination: what you compared, the numbers, any adjustments and your conclusion.

example.title: One quote for a pump
example.body: You get one quote, $18,400, for a replacement pump. The office bought the same model 14 months ago for $16,900. Adjusting for about 4% price growth gives roughly $17,600, and the manufacturer's catalog lists $18,250 plus shipping. The quote is in line with the market. You document both comparisons and conclude the price is fair and reasonable.

remember: Price analysis = compare prices; cost analysis = examine costs and profit.
Competition and prior prices are the strongest evidence.
mistakes: Comparing only with the IGCE when real market prices are available.
Forgetting to adjust prior prices for time and quantity.

title: Cost analysis, certified data and cost principles
summary: On large sole-source or noncompetitive buys, the Government may need the contractor's certified cost or pricing data and must look at each element of cost. Cost principles decide which costs the Government will pay.
why: Cost analysis and FAR Part 31 (Contract Cost Principles and Procedures, on the exam list) round out the pricing questions. The DoW threshold for certified data changed in 2026.

sections.body:
Under the Truthful Cost or Pricing Data statute (often still called TINA), the contracting officer must get certified cost or pricing data before awarding a contract or modification above a threshold, unless an exception applies.
- FAR threshold: $2.5 million (FAR 15.403-3).
- **DoW:** $10 million for prime contracts awarded after 30 June 2026, under the FY2026 NDAA and DFARS 215.403-3 class deviation. Contracts awarded on or before that date keep $2.5 million.

The contractor certifies the data are accurate, complete and current (15.403-4). If they were not, the Government can reduce the price (defective pricing).

- **Direct costs:** tied to the contract, such as direct labor and materials.
- **Indirect costs:** shared across work, such as overhead and general and administrative (G&A) expenses, applied through rates.
- **Profit or fee:** DoW uses a structured method, the weighted guidelines, to set profit objectives on many noncompetitive actions (DFARS Subpart 215.4).
- **Cost realism:** on cost-type contracts, check whether proposed costs are realistic for the work, because the Government pays actual costs (FAR 15.404-3).
Ask for audit and pricing support on big actions: the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) audits proposals and contractor systems, and price analysts in your command can help.

example.title: Sole-source spare parts
example.body: A $14 million sole-source contract for aircraft spare parts awarded in October 2026 is above the DoW $10 million threshold, there is no competition and the parts are not commercial. You request certified cost or pricing data, ask DCAA for an audit, and analyze labor rates, material costs, overhead and profit before negotiating.

remember: Allowable = reasonable + allocable + standards + terms + not prohibited.
DoW TINA: $10M for awards after 30 June 2026; FAR text still says $2.5M.
mistakes: Requiring certified data on a competitive or commercial buy.
Paying for entertainment or alcohol as a contract cost.
verify: The $10 million DoW threshold comes from 10 U.S.C. 3702 as amended by the FY2026 NDAA and DoW's DFARS Part 215 class deviation. Subcontract flow-down figures in that deviation differ in places; check them before quoting a subcontract number.

title: Negotiation
summary: Negotiation is planned, not improvised. Set objectives backed by analysis, know your limits and your alternatives, communicate clearly, and write down what was agreed and why.
why: Plan Negotiation is 10 exam questions, and negotiation skills pay off on every modification and sole-source buy you handle.

sections.body:
- Analyze the proposal (price, cost, technical) and the risks.
- Set **prenegotiation objectives**: the price and terms you aim for, based on your analysis. Larger actions need them documented and approved (FAR 15.408-1).
- Decide your minimum and maximum positions and the issues that matter most.
- Know your **BATNA**, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you will do if talks fail.
- Agree on team roles: who leads, who takes notes, who answers technical questions.

sections.h: Exchanges with offerors in a competition
sections.body:
In competitive Part 15 buys, exchanges are tightly controlled:
- **Clarifications:** limited exchanges to clear up minor issues when award is planned without negotiations (FAR 15.202(a)(2)).
- **Competitive range:** the most highly rated proposals, set when negotiations will be held (15.204-1).
- **Negotiations** (formerly called discussions) with each offeror in the competitive range: point out significant weaknesses and deficiencies and give a chance to revise (15.204-2).
Do not reveal one offeror's information or price to another, and treat offerors equally.

- Open with clear, well-supported positions.
- Focus on interests (why each side wants something), not just positions.
- Trade concessions; never give something for nothing.
- Use facts from your analysis, not emotion.
- Summarize agreements as you go and confirm them in writing.

The **price negotiation memorandum (PNM)** records the purpose, the objectives, what was proposed, what was agreed, and how the agreement compares with the objectives, with explanations for the differences (15.408-2). It is the main evidence that the price is fair and reasonable.

example.title: The modification
example.body: A contractor proposes $212,000 for added work. Your analysis supports $180,000 to $195,000; your objective is $185,000. In negotiation they show a material quote you had not seen, so you move up; you hold firm on an inflated labor rate. You settle at $191,000, within your range, and the PNM explains each movement.

remember: Clarification is not negotiation, and neither is a chance to rewrite a proposal unless negotiations are held.
mistakes: Telling one offeror where its price stands against a competitor's.

title: Source selection: choosing the winner
summary: In a negotiated competition you evaluate every proposal only against the factors the solicitation stated, then the source selection authority decides which offer is the best value and writes down why. The winner must also be found responsible.
why: Select Source is 10 exam questions, and the exam FAQ says many questions come from FAR Part 15. Source selection mistakes are the main cause of sustained protests.

sections.body: The **source selection authority (SSA)** makes the decision; on many buys the contracting officer is the SSA. Evaluators (often a source selection evaluation board) rate proposals against the stated factors. The contracting officer is the focal point for all exchanges with offerors (FAR 15.201).

The best value can be reached different ways (FAR 15.103):
- **Tradeoff:** the Government may pay more for a better technical offer, if the benefit is worth the price (15.103-1).
- **Lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA):** award to the lowest-priced offer that meets every requirement; no tradeoffs (15.103-2). DoW limits when LPTA may be used (DFARS 215.103-2-70).
- **Highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price** and **phased acquisitions** are also available (15.103-3, 15.103-4).

The solicitation states the factors and their relative importance (FAR 15.104):
- **Price or cost** is always evaluated.
- **Past performance** is usually evaluated on larger buys.
- **Technical or management** factors as needed.
Evaluate proposals **only** on the stated factors (15.202). Evaluating something not in the solicitation is a common reason protests succeed.

The Government may award without negotiations if the solicitation said it might (15.203); otherwise it sets a competitive range and negotiates (15.204). The SSA's decision must be the SSA's own judgment, based on a comparison of proposals against the criteria, and documented, including why any higher price was worth paying (15.205).

No award goes to a contractor unless the contracting officer affirmatively determines it is responsible (FAR 9.103). The general standards (9.104-1) include adequate financial resources, the ability to meet the schedule, a satisfactory performance record, a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics, and the needed organization, skills, equipment and facilities. Check SAM for exclusions: excluded contractors generally cannot receive new awards (9.404, 9.405).

example.title: Paying more for better
example.body: Offeror A is rated Outstanding technically at $4.8 million; Offeror B is Acceptable at $4.3 million. Under a tradeoff, the SSA explains in writing that A's approach cuts a key risk to the mission and that the $500,000 difference is worth it. Without that written reasoning, the award would be easy to protest.

remember: Evaluate only what you said you would, the way you said you would.
Best value decision + responsibility determination = award.
mistakes: Awarding before checking SAM exclusions and responsibility.

title: Award, notices and debriefings
summary: After the decision, award the contract, tell the offerors who did not win, and, when they ask in time, debrief them on why. Debriefings done well prevent protests; done badly they start them.
why: Notifying and debriefing offerors is a Select Source job task and shows up in both award and protest questions. FAC 082 covers it before CON 1300V.

sections.body: Award by sending the contract or award notice to the winner. Report the action in the Government's contract reporting system, now part of SAM.gov (FAR 4.301). Larger awards (above $5.5 million under the RFO FAR) are also publicly announced on the day of award (FAR 5.302).

- **Preaward notices:** tell offerors excluded from the competitive range or otherwise eliminated, promptly and in writing (FAR 15.206-1).
- **Award notice:** within 3 days after award, notify each offeror in the competitive range that was not selected: how many offers were solicited and received, the winner's name, the award price and, in general terms, why their proposal was not accepted (15.207-2).

- **Preaward debriefing:** an offeror excluded before award may ask within 3 days of the notice (15.206-2).
- **Postaward debriefing:** an offeror that asks in writing within 3 days of receiving the award notice must be debriefed, within 5 days of the request to the maximum extent practicable (15.301-1).
- A debriefing explains the Government's evaluation of the offeror's significant weaknesses or deficiencies, the overall ratings and prices of the winner and the debriefed offeror, the rankings if any, a summary of the rationale for award, and answers to relevant questions.
- It must **not** reveal other offerors' trade secrets, confidential commercial information or proposal details, or make point-by-point comparisons with other proposals.
- DoW adds enhanced debriefing rules, including a chance for follow-up questions (DFARS 215.301-70 and 215.301-71).
A protest filed at GAO within 5 days after a required debriefing triggers an automatic stay of performance, so debriefing dates directly affect your schedule (see the protests lesson).

example.title: A good debriefing
example.body: The losing offeror asks for a debriefing the day after the award notice. Within five days you walk through its significant weaknesses, its ratings and price compared with the winner's, and the reasons for the award, and you answer its questions without revealing the winner's proposal details. The company understands the decision and decides not to protest.

remember: Award notice within 3 days; debriefing request within 3 days; debrief within 5 days.
Explain the decision; never reveal another offeror's proposal.
mistakes: Sharing the winner's technical approach in a debriefing.

title: Protests
summary: A protest is a written objection by an interested party to a solicitation or an award. It can be filed with the agency, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the Court of Federal Claims. Strict deadlines apply, and a timely GAO protest can stop the contract in its tracks.
why: Manage Disagreements is 10 exam questions, and FAR Part 33 (Protests, Disputes, and Appeals) is on the exam list.

sections.body:
- A protest about something wrong on the face of the solicitation must be filed **before** bid opening or the closing date for proposals.
- Other protests generally must be filed within **10 days** after the basis was known or should have been known.
- When a debriefing is required and requested, a protest about matters raised in it can be filed within **5 days** after the debriefing.
- GAO decides within **100 days**. The agency files its report within 30 days.

When GAO tells the agency of a protest:
- before award, the contract may not be awarded;
- after award, performance must be suspended if the protest was filed within 10 days after award or within 5 days after a required debriefing, whichever is later.
The head of the contracting activity can override the stay in writing in limited circumstances (urgent and compelling, or in the best interest of the Government after award). For an agency-level protest filed in time, performance is also generally suspended (33.104-3). The agency tries to resolve agency protests within 35 days (33.104-4(c)(1)).

Protests of orders under indefinite-delivery contracts are limited: for DoW, GAO hears protests of orders valued above $35 million, or protests that an order increases the scope, period or maximum value of the contract (FAR 16.508).

Tell your contracting officer and legal counsel at once, preserve the entire file, follow the stay rules, and do not discuss the protest with the protester or the awardee outside proper channels. Often the best response is corrective action: fixing a real mistake quickly.

example.title: Clock math
example.body: Award is made 1 March. The losing offeror requests a debriefing on time and is debriefed 6 March. It files at GAO on 10 March, within 5 days after the debriefing, so performance must be suspended even though it is more than 10 days after award. Mark both dates in the file as soon as you know them.

remember: Solicitation problems: before closing. Everything else: 10 days, or 5 days after a required debriefing.
GAO: 100 days to decide; the stay depends on filing within 10 days of award or 5 days of the debriefing.
mistakes: Letting the awardee keep working after a timely GAO protest without an approved override.
Throwing away notes or emails after a protest is filed.
